1.pericope_label: O that thou wouldest rend the heavens and come down
debates: What the melting fire of the second verse denotes
Whether the coming prayed for is the incarnation, the last judgment, or a present deliverance
Whether the repeated clause in the third verse is accidental or deliberate
outliers: Clarke holds the text of the second verse to be much corrupted, since the ancient versions preserve no trace of either interpretation on offer
themes: A prayer continued across a chapter division
Deliverance asked for openly enough that others must see it
Sinai remembered as the pattern of what is asked
Precedent used as the ground of petition

4.pericope_label: Since the beginning of the world men have not heard
debates: How the apostolic citation relates to the Hebrew text
Whether the fifth verse continues the retrospect or expresses a wish
What the final clause of the fifth verse means
outliers: Clarke pronounces the last clause utterly unintelligible as it stands and reconstructs it by conjecture
themes: Blessing beyond what any faculty could anticipate
A God known by what he does for those who wait
Joy and right action named as one thing
Confession breaking into the middle of a plea

6.pericope_label: All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags
debates: Whether the uncleanness named is leprosy or another ceremonial defilement
Whether none at all called upon God or comparatively few
Whether the last clause means consumed us or handed us over
outliers: Clarke rebukes preachers for using the phrase filthy rags without knowing what the word denotes
themes: Confession as the preparation for deliverance
No one left fit to intercede
Sin punished by being handed back to itself
A remnant praying that the whole nation may be included

8.pericope_label: Thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter
debates: Whether the verse opens with but now or with and thou
What the image of the potter is meant to establish
On what ground the appeal for mercy rests
outliers: Ellicott makes the potter image a ground of prayer rather than of submission, against the sense it usually carries
themes: A relation surviving what has been done to it
Sovereignty pleaded as a reason for hope
Wrath deprecated in degree and not in principle
A claim resting on covenant rather than desert

10.pericope_label: Thy holy cities are a wilderness; wilt thou refrain thyself?
debates: Why the holy cities are named in the plural
Whether the pleasant things are parts of the temple or the buildings of the city
Which temple the house refers to
outliers: Gill takes the burnt house to be the second temple, where Ellicott sees the destruction of the first foreseen in vision
themes: Holiness extending from the land to its cities
A ruin presented as a claim on God
The temple as the climax of the lament
A prayer ending on an unanswered question
